newsitem.title: USA: Suit filed to halt immigrant cutoff under welfare.
newsitem.headline: Suit filed to halt immigrant cutoff under welfare.

text.p: Advocates for the poor filed a class-action lawsuit Wednesday seeking to overturn a new welfare law that cuts off federal nutrition and disability aid to legal immigrants.

Public-interest law offices filed suit in federal district court in New York on behalf of about 100,000 legal immigrants in New York, Vermont and Connecticut who face elimination of Food Stamps and Supplemental Security Income disability aid.
They argue that the law violates the constitutional guarantee of equal protection for all persons. A second suit is expected to be filed in San Fransisco.

"The Constitution's guarantee of equal protection under the laws does not permit Congress to selectively target legal permanent residents who are impoverished, disabled and elderly," Nancy Chang of the Center for Constitutional Rights said in a statement.

The federal government has begun mailing out notices to hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants, warning them they could lose disability benefits by this August. The SSI program provides monthly checks to the disabled or elderly.
Legal immigrants will also begin losing eligibility for Food Stamps under the law, starting in April.
Congressional Republicans who crafted the welfare law argue noncitizens should not be entitled to federal benefits.
They also say that because state welfare rolls are falling, governors will have more money than expected under the new law to aid any immigrants who may be affected.
But under continuing pressure from governors of states such as New York and Florida with large immigrant populations, Republicans have said they may set up a special fund to aid some immigrants.
President Clinton, who signed the law, has asked Congress to restore about $14 billion in aid to legal residents.

One of those represented in the suit is Ekaterina Drubich, an 87-year-old Holocaust survivor who left the former Soviet Union in 1980. She is partially paralyzed, has had a mastectomy and is too frail to travel on her own.
"I find it inconceivable that the same country that welcomed me as a refugee would allow me to go hungry and homeless," Drubich said in a statement.
